takeaway: LiqSD makes exabyte-scale DNA look like a 4 KB block device by keeping a coarse map on SSD and appending fine maps, data, and garbage-collection traces to DNA.
background: DNA could preserve enormous archives for centuries, but synthesis, sequencing, and erasure operate at coarse molecular units with tens-of-minutes latency. A conventional block interface needs fine updates and address translation across exabyte capacity without petabytes of fast metadata.
villain: A flat 4 KB mapping table is too large, while a coarse mapping requires reading and rewriting a roughly 24 MB synthesis cluster for a tiny update. In-place DNA updates and garbage collection amplify sequencing and synthesis by orders of magnitude.
approach: LiqSD uses a dual translation layer: SSD stores logical-section mappings, while DNA stores append-only per-block patches and data. Garbage-collection relocation metadata is encoded symbiotically with moved blocks, and invalidation is delayed until translation pages are read. A cache loads all useful blocks from a sequenced cluster, while SSD redo logs make DNA operations crash-consistent.
impact: The design is an exploration of the abstraction boundary for molecular storage, identifying metadata and update mechanisms that remain plausible at exabyte scale. It demonstrates access amplification rather than claiming current DNA is a low-latency device.

evaluation.overview: A DNA-media simulator runs sequential/random microbenchmarks and five cloud, server, and archival traces, measuring read/write amplification, GC, delayed invalidation, block size, space, and qualitative latency.
evaluation.implemented: An open-source LiqSD simulator and block interface with Reed–Solomon/rotation coding, plus a FUSE and Ext4 stack used to run Vim.
evaluation.setting: A dual-24-core Xeon Gold 5317 server with 188 GB DRAM and 7 TB NVMe; simulated DNA uses 296-nucleotide strands, 4 KB blocks, 40% coding redundancy, and a 120 MB cache.
baselines: naive DNA device without translation layer

results.text: On real traces, LiqSD reports up to 2,927× lower write amplification than compared DNA-device designs; microbenchmark reductions reach roughly seven orders of magnitude.
The customized cluster-aware cache cuts read amplification by up to 6,206× in microbenchmarks and 7× on real traces, with over 99.3% of L1 translation reads cached.
LiqSD's fine translation and garbage-collection metadata add an estimated 3.1% DNA-space overhead, while delayed invalidation avoids translation reads during writes.

limitations: No wet-lab DNA experiment is performed; the simulator counts strands and injects errors, so evaluation centers on relative amplification rather than physical throughput, cost, or full queueing behavior. Current-technology estimates remain about 49 minutes per block read and 74 minutes per write. GC can exhaust capacity for high-validity traces, and SSD metadata still requires migration or RAID protection.
phd_group_signal: The paper chooses metrics suited to an immature medium, builds a cross-technology hierarchy, and states where simulation ends and chemistry begins. It is a strong example of exploratory storage research that tests an abstraction before the hardware is operationally mature.

claims.text: The SSD-resident L0 table maps logical to physical sections, while append-only DNA-resident L1 patches resolve 4 KB blocks without rewriting a whole synthesis cluster.
Symbiotic relocation records embedded with moved data let recovery reconstruct garbage-collection history, and delayed invalidation postpones obsolete-block discovery to existing reads.
